{{Short description|Game theory}}

'''Program equilibrium''' is a [[game theory | game-theoretic]] [[solution concept]] for a scenario in which players submit computer programs to play the game on their behalf and the programs can read each other's source code. The term was introduced by [[Moshe Tennenholtz]] in 2004.<ref name="Tennenholtz2004" /> The same setting had previously been studied by [[R. Preston McAfee]],<ref name="McAfee1984" /> J. V. Howard<ref name="Howard1988" /> and [[Ariel Rubinstein]].<ref name="Rubinstein1998" />

== Setting and definition ==

The program equilibrium literature considers the following setting. Consider a [[normal-form game]] as a base game. For simplicity, consider a two-player game in which <math>S_1</math> and <math>S_2</math> are the sets of available [[strategy (game theory) | strategies]] and <math>u_1</math> and <math>u_2</math> are the players' [[Utility#Functions | utility functions]]. Then we construct a new (normal-form) ''program game'' in which each player <math>i</math> chooses a computer program <math>p_i</math>. The payoff (utility) for the players is then determined as follows. Each player's program <math>p_i</math> is run with the other program <math>p_{-i}</math> as input and outputs a strategy <math>s_i</math> for Player <math>i</math>. For convenience one also often imagines that programs can access their own source code.{{refn|group=nb|It is not necessary for programs in the program game to be given access to their own source code. By the [[diagonalization lemma]], one can use [[Quine (computing) | quining]] to enable programs to refer to their source code.<ref name="McAfee1984" /><ref name="Howard1988" /><ref name="Rubinstein1998" />}} Finally, the utilities for the players are given by <math>u_i(s_1,s_2)</math> for <math>i=1,2</math>, i.e., by applying the utility functions for the base game to the chosen strategies.

One has to further deal with the possibility that one of the programs <math>p_i</math> doesn't halt. One way to deal with this is to restrict both players' sets of available programs to prevent non-halting programs.<ref name="Tennenholtz2004" /><ref name="Oesterheld2019" />

A program equilibrium is a pair of programs <math>(p_1,p_2)</math> that constitute a [[Nash equilibrium]] of the program game. In other words, <math>(p_1,p_2)</math> is a program equilibrium if neither player <math>i</math> can deviate to an alternative program <math>p_i'</math> such that their utility is higher in <math>(p_i',p_{-i})</math> than in <math>(p_1,p_2)</math>.

Instead of programs, some authors have the players submit other kinds of objects, such as logical formulas specifying what action to play depending on an encoding of the logical formula submitted by the opponent.<ref name="Hoek2013" /><ref name="PetersSzentes2012" />

== Different mechanisms for achieving cooperative program equilibrium in the Prisoner's Dilemma ==

Various authors have proposed ways to achieve cooperative program equilibrium in the [[Prisoner's Dilemma]].

=== Cooperation based on syntactic comparison === 

Multiple authors have independently proposed the following program for the Prisoner's Dilemma:<ref name="Tennenholtz2004" /><ref name="Howard1988" /><ref name="McAfee1984" />

 '''algorithm''' CliqueBot(opponent_program):
     '''if''' opponent_program == this_program '''then'''
         '''return''' Cooperate
     '''else'''
         '''return''' Defect

If both players submit this program, then the if-clause will resolve to true in the execution of both programs. As a result, both programs will cooperate. Moreover, (CliqueBot,CliqueBot) is an equilibrium. If either player deviates to some other program <math>p_i</math> that is different from CliqueBot, then the opponent will defect. Therefore, deviating to <math>p_i</math> can at best result in the payoff of mutual defection, which is worse than the payoff of mutual cooperation.

This approach has been criticized for being fragile.<ref name="Oesterheld2019" /> If the players fail to coordinate on the exact source code they submit (for example, if one player adds an extra space character), both programs will defect. The development of the techniques below is in part motivated by this fragility issue.

=== Proof-based cooperation ===

Another approach is based on letting each player's program try to prove something about the opponent's program or about how the two programs relate.<ref name="Hoek2013" /><ref name="Barasz2014" /><ref name="Critch2019" /><ref name="Critch2022" /> One example of such a program is the following:

 '''algorithm''' FairBot(opponent_program):
     '''if''' there is a proof that opponent_program(this_program) = Cooperate '''then'''
         '''return''' Cooperate
     '''else'''
         '''return''' Defect

Using [[Löb's theorem]] it can be shown that when both players submit this program, they cooperate against each other.<ref name="Barasz2014" /><ref name="Critch2019" /><ref name="Critch2022" /> Moreover, if one player were to instead submit a program that defects against the above program, then (assuming consistency of the proof system is used) the if-condition would resolve to false and the above program would defect. Therefore, (FairBot,FairBot) is a program equilibrium as well.

=== Cooperating with ε-grounded simulation ===

Another proposed program is the following:<ref name="Oesterheld2019" /><ref name="DiGiovanni2023" /><ref name="Cooper2025" />

 '''algorithm''' <math>\epsilon</math>GroundedFairBot(opponent_program):
     With probability <math>\epsilon</math>:
         '''return''' Cooperate
     '''return''' opponent_program(this_program)

Here <math>\epsilon</math> is a small{{quantify|date=March 2025}} positive number.

If both players submit this program, then they terminate [[almost surely]] and cooperate. The expected number of steps to termination is given by the [[geometric series]]. Moreover, if both players submit this program, neither can profitably deviate, assuming <math>\epsilon</math> is sufficiently small{{quantify|date=March 2025}}, because defecting with probability <math>\Delta</math> would cause the opponent to defect with probability <math>(1-\epsilon)\Delta</math>.

== Folk theorem ==

We here give a theorem that characterizes what payoffs can be achieved in program equilibrium.

The theorem uses the following terminology: A pair of payoffs <math>(v_1,v_2)</math> is called ''feasible'' if there is a pair of [[strategy (game theory) | (potentially mixed) strategies]] <math>(s_1,s_2)</math> such that <math>u_i(s_1,s_2)=v_i</math> for both players <math>i</math>. That is, a pair of payoffs is called feasible if it is achieved in some [[strategy profile]]. A payoff <math>v_i</math> is called ''[[folk theorem (game theory)#Setup and definitions | individually rational]]'' if it is better than that player's minimax payoff; that is, if <math>v_i \geq \min_{\sigma_{-i}}\max_{s_{i}} u_i(\sigma_{-i},s_{i})</math>, where the minimum is over all mixed strategies for Player <math>-i</math>.{{refn|group=nb|Equivalently, (by [[John von Neumann | von Neumann]]'s [[minimax theorem]]), <math>v_i \geq \max_{\sigma_i}\min_{s_{-i}} u_i(\sigma_i,s_{-i})</math>, where the maximum is over all mixed strategies <math>\sigma_i</math> for Player <math>i</math>.}}

'''Theorem''' (folk theorem for program equilibrium):<ref name="Rubinstein1998" /><ref name="Tennenholtz2004" /> Let G be a base game. Let <math>(v_1,v_2)</math> be a pair of real-valued payoffs. Then the following two claims are equivalent:
* The payoffs <math>(v_1,v_2)</math> are feasible and individually rational.
* There is a program equilibrium <math>(p_1,p_2)</math> that achieves payoffs <math>(v_1,v_2)</math>.

The result is referred to as a ''folk theorem'' in reference to the so-called [[folk theorem (game theory) | folk theorems (game theory)]] for [[repeated games]], which use the same conditions on equilibrium payoffs <math>(v_1,v_2)</math>.
